item.title: The Tory war on Neets will punish parents instead
item.dc:creator: Rachel Cunliffe
item.description: At what age is a person no longer considered the responsibility of their parents?
item.content:encoded: At what age is a person no longer considered the responsibility of their parents? In the past, 18 was the obvious answer. But in our modern era of rising rents and graduates struggling to find work after university, it can seem as if young people are experiencing a kind of prolonged adolescence. Luckily for the youth, the Conservative Party has teased a modest proposal in the run-up to its conference. The headline idea is standard right-wing schtick – or, as the shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately euphemistically put it, “tough love”. Instead of Universal Credit, unemployed under-25s who are deemed fit to work would receive a “Get to Work Allowance” rather than the current benefits, requiring them to jump through various hoops to prove they are really trying to find a job. If they are still jobless after six months their allowance would be cut by 30 per cent.

item.title: Joyce Carol Oates contradicts herself
item.dc:creator: George Monaghan
item.description: How can the author of 100 books have "no personality"?
item.content:encoded: “He’s sort of talking. He’s sort of distracting to me. He seems to be sort of talking to himself.”

item.title: How to die well
item.dc:creator: Grace Bishop
item.description: Nicole Kidman and Caroline Lucas are doing it. What are "death doulas" and why should we trust them to help us die?
item.content:encoded: In the final moments of a person’s life, you might hope to take one last look at the people closest to you – friends, family, lovers. But what if you saw Nicole Kidman? Her pale skin and light blue eyes staring down at you, as you pass from this life to the next.

item.title: Jewish Greens divided over “Zionism is racism” motion
item.dc:creator: Megan Kenyon
item.description: The motion has opened a rift at the heart of the party
item.content:encoded: Green Party members descended on Brighton on Friday (2 October) for the party’s annual conference. As well as gathering to listen to speeches by the party’s leadership team and its MPs, members will vote on motions which are designed to change, update or introduce party policies.

item.title: Zack Polanski: The Greens can change the government
item.dc:creator: Megan Kenyon
item.description: In his conference speech, the Green leader argued his party has held Labour's worst instincts in check
item.content:encoded: Zack Polanski only spent a few hours at his second party conference as leader before hopping on the train back to London to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras. The party has encouraged members to do the same. An internal briefing seen by the New Statesman and sent out to party members said the campaign team needs at least 1,000 Green members out on the doorsteps every day until Thursday (8 October) to get the vote out. It described the race as being on a “knife edge”.

item.title: Katherine Rundell: AI’s greasy little voice is built on stolen labour
item.dc:creator: New Statesman
item.description: The author and academic is worried about how AI will affect children's ability to learn
item.content:encoded: This week, the author and academic Katherine Rundell was interviewed by our culture editor Tanjil Rashid on the New Statesman‘s weekly culture podcast The New Society. In comments that have generated wide-ranging discussion online, Rundell discussed her fears about AI “pillaging” writers’ work as well as destroying children’s ability to learn. item.title: Sheep will be provided
item.dc:creator: Rachel Cunliffe
item.description: One day a year, the countryside comes to the City of London
item.content:encoded: The views from Southwark Bridge are something to behold: St Paul’s Cathedral, majestic city skyscrapers, the Tate Modern’s soaring chimney… and the sheep. There are nine of them, mildly ambling down the pavement of the bridge in the shadow of the Shard. They are the calmest thing about this scene, which includes crowds of camera-wielding spectators shouting encouragement as figures in bright red robes urge them (the sheep, that is, not the spectators) across the river. The cycle lane has been co-opted as a pen for the next batch of wannabe-shepherds, who have been corralled there to wait for their turn at sheep driving.

item.title: Celebrity Traitors has tamed our national id
item.dc:creator: Finn McRedmond
item.description: The show's cultural dominance proves that we are all deferential homebodies
item.content:encoded: Television used to hold a mirror up to the nation. When X-Factor was at the height of its powers in the late 2000s, this was a land of optimists who understood the moral of Simon Cowell’s universe: the right amount of talent, ambition and cruelty could take anyone to the stratosphere, or at least a brief stint at Christmas number one. The difficulties of the intervening decade stamped out that mode of aspiration, naturally. And, well, who has spoken of X-Factor since 2012?

item.title: How I escaped the Labour Party Conference
item.dc:creator: Pippa Bailey
item.description: I had to get out of the forbidding maze of lanyards, parties and Harold Wilson
item.content:encoded: Twelve hours into my first Labour conference, and I have the curious sensation of having gone back in time a few decades, to my first day of secondary school. The conference centre is alienatingly huge, and I wear holes in the carpet trying to find my way between rooms with names like “2C” and “11B”, up and down escalators, round and round corridors. Everyone else seems somehow bigger than me, and they not only know where they are going, but also all know each other. My bag is too heavy. I am at all times either lost or late, and often both.

item.title: Electoral reform could kill the Labour Party
item.dc:creator: Ben Walker
item.description: Has Andy Burnham opened Pandora's box?
item.content:encoded: It’s the announcement that may just kill off the Labour Party as we know it – a national commission on electoral reform. Andy Burnham told the Labour party conference that he would fight the next election on a pledge to change how the nation votes. In the past he has indicated a preference for proportional representation. He’s not the first Labour Party leader to make this promise (Blair’s 1997 manifesto pledge springs to mind), but, for now, let’s take him at his word.

item.title: Emma Cline and the perverse silence of dying
item.dc:creator: Abhrajyoti Chakraborty
item.description: Cline’s new novel Switzy follows a wealthy man’s last days as he heads to a euthanasia clinic
item.content:encoded: David Hastings, the retired corporate executive protagonist of Switzy, Emma Cline’s new, Booker Prize longlisted novel, always carries a small leather notebook in his jacket pocket. When he wakes up in the mornings, he opens it up to recall his own name, the names of his daughter (Rebecca) and grandson (Rainer), his itinerary over the next week or so – all scribbled down in a patchy handwriting that must be his but he still can’t recognise. His 30-something assistant Cody is “the real keeper of the schedule, but it was one of those little feints they made at normalcy”. Not too long ago, David was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s. His doctor had told him there was no cure: the best therapies merely stave off the worst symptoms. To David, the plodding progression of the disease seemed particularly dreadful, the ignominy of bearing witness to steadily losing one’s mind.

item.title: From the archive: Jim Callaghan’s still small voice
item.dc:creator: James Fenton
item.description: March 1978: Does Labour need to refresh its mandate?
item.content:encoded: In March 1978, the minority Labour government’s pact with David Steel’s Liberals, which was helping keep it in office, was strained. A snap election looked plausible. In the New Statesman, the journalist and poet James Fenton considered the case for James Callaghan going to the country.

item.title: There’s big trouble in Little Portugal
item.dc:creator: Finn McRedmond
item.description: Salted cod and sandwiches doused in gravy?
item.content:encoded: As with everything that happened before 1980, we can blame God. I am talking, of course, about the Portuguese zeal for salted cod. Catholics used to have very strict rules about when they could eat meat, and so fish was a handy alternative. But, as fellow enthusiasts of the EU Common Fisheries Policy will know, Atlantic cod do not actually live near Portugal. They were caught, preserved in salt to survive the import journey, and eaten in Lisbon on a Friday.

item.title: Patricia Lockwood: “You know how women marry their dads? I married my mother”
item.dc:creator: Emily Lawford
item.description: The poet and novelist on judging the Booker and America's insanity
item.content:encoded: “This is the full butthole horse,” Patricia Lockwood says, pointing to a painting of a stallion’s flared behind. “He needs you to see his orifice. He’s really proud of it. It’s like, powering him on his journey.”

item.title: Why men can’t ask women out any more
item.dc:creator: Oli Dugmore
item.description: We need to address the flirting recession
item.content:encoded: With some surprise, I recently discovered that I have acquired something quite remarkable: status. How did this happy development come about, I hear you ask? Through wealth or fame, professional achievement or acts of charity? No, of course not. I acquired this magical virtue simply by entering a new aspirational class of people: those with more than one child.

item.title: Donald Trump is sick of his job
item.dc:creator: Freddie Hayward
item.description: The President appears to be bored by his duties
item.content:encoded: Republicans in Washington often speak with a wistful air about Donald Trump’s first term. The reminisces are simple: a decent economy, strong borders and no new foreign wars. Of course, there was the bombast and craziness that upended the usual way that presidents composed themselves, as well as weekly scandals, and the two impeachments. But some consider that a necessary jolt to establishment malaise, a defibrillation of the American political system.

item.title: We have all desecrated Diana
item.dc:creator: Zoë Huxford
item.description: A showcase of her "revenge dress" proves Charles Spencer is not the first to distort her memory
item.content:encoded: A black silk crepe dress, measuring a petite 78cm at the bust, 74cm at the waist and 82cm at the hip, with a pleated bodice, off-the-shoulder neckline and chiffon train. Among all the fragments of celebrity culture, few have been reproduced with as much dedication as what most of us call Princess Diana’s “revenge dress”, and which Tina Brown called her “fuck-you dress”. As her ex-husband and her brother feud over her legacy, an afterlife that is bizarrely claimed by King-hating republicans and monarchists alike, it seems that she and her clothes remain immovable symbols in our collective life and memory.

item.title: My life is tough, but at least there isn’t a crack den on my street
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Lezard
item.description: And these people are not the nice, polite kind of crackhead
item.content:encoded: It has been a slow news week in this column; all I have done is go back and forth from Brighton to East Finchley, with daily trips to the Whittington to check on my mother, and hourly visits to the kitchen cupboard to pour Sheba into the cat’s bowl. Even I am getting bored of this and until there is a new development I don’t see how I can get an amusing, or even interesting, column out of it.

item.title: Barack Obama’s reading list
item.dc:creator: Rachel Cunliffe
item.description: Has it really only been ten years since he was president?
item.content:encoded: How soothing it is to hear Barack Obama’s rousing yet dulcet tones again. “We are living through some tumultuous times,” the 44th president of the United States begins. “Change is coming at us faster than ever.” To weather it, we need a strong moral framework for ourselves – to find ways to work together, bridge divides and learn to see things from another point of view. How do we do this?

item.title: Possessed by Edgar Allan Poe
item.dc:creator: James Marcus
item.description: Poe's work owes its greatest debt to his unconscious, where his deepest anxieties lay
item.content:encoded: One summer day in 1849, Edgar Allan Poe arrived on the Philadelphia doorstep of a friend and former colleague named John Sartain. The 40-year-old author, who would be dead within the year, was in awful shape. As he explained to his host, he had been travelling south by train to Richmond, Virginia, when he overheard a sinister group of men plotting to kill him. To evade them, he disembarked, made his way to Philadelphia, spent several days on a drunken bender and was briefly deposited in prison. Sartain was glad to offer him shelter. Yet he was frightened by his guest’s hallucinatory chatter, along with his suicidal impulses: first Poe asked to borrow a straight razor, then he seemed intent on jumping from a high platform the two men visited later that night.
